raw_response:
Ai, sit down, let me think this through. It's that time of year again — the wheat is getting tall in the fields, and the ground is warming up enough that I need to start thinking about the cotton. My old man and I are the only ones in the house now — the children went off to work in the city years back. At 76 my knees hurt climbing out to the field, but I still go every day. We have to keep it simple.

Six and a half mu, that's our land. I split it the way I always have: about 5 mu together for the wheat and corn — that's the double-crop, what everyone in our village does — and the other 1.5 mu, the sandy piece out by the road, I put in cotton. I used to grow more cotton when I was younger and stronger, but the picking is hard on the back. 1.5 mu I can still manage with my sister-in-law coming to help in the busy season.

**Wheat** — it's been in the ground since last October. When I planted I put one bag of compound fertilizer per mu, that 15-15-15 stuff the village shop sells. Then in March when the wheat turned green again I scattered about half a bag of urea. Now it's jointing, looks alright to me. If the heads come out pale I might throw a bit more urea on, but I probably won't — fertilizer went up again this year. We had good rain in winter so I've only watered twice. Maybe one more time when the grain fills in May, if it stays dry. The well pump costs more every year, electricity isn't free. In June the combine driver comes through the village and cuts it for us — 50 yuan a mu, but there's no way I can cut by hand anymore.

**Maize** — soon as the wheat comes off, same day or the next, I call the fellow with the planter and he drills the maize seed. Window is tight, only a few days. I buy the hybrid seed from the shop — whatever Zhengdan variety the shopkeeper pushes is usually fine. One bag of compound when he plants, and I'll scatter a bit of urea when the corn is about knee-high, if it looks like it needs it. Maize doesn't need as much babying as wheat. Maybe one watering in August if there's a dry spell. Harvest end of September, the machine guy again.

**Cotton** — this is the hard one. I'll plant by hand in the last week of April, my husband drops the seeds and I cover them. One bag of compound per mu at planting, and a little urea at squaring. I spray for aphids and bollworm when I see them — the village agent tells us when to spray, I just follow what the neighbors are doing. Cotton picking starts in September, goes all through October, three, four pickings. That's where the hired help comes in — I pay my sister-in-law and the neighbor girl 80 yuan a day.

Money is always tight. I figure I have maybe four thousand yuan for the whole year's inputs, stretching it. If I was younger and had more money I'd probably put more fertilizer down, the agricultural station people always say we under-apply, but I'm not going to borrow at my age.
